Items.Authors: Maurizio Oliviero, Roberto Speziali, Francesco Bianchi, Sergio Musmeci, Felice Pignatiello, Andrea Di Paola, Luciano Terranegra
Items.Title: SPACE-MOF: a first step towards an imaging MOF for space applications
Items.Abstract: We present a Magneto-Optical Filter (MOF) developed for space applications, capable of capturing images of the solar atmosphere in intensity, Doppler velocity, and line-of-sight magnetic field components. Our MOF addresses limitations of prior versions with key enhancements: a novel welding technique for optical windows to endure launch-induced mechanical stresses and thermal variations, and an expanded clear aperture for high-resolution full-disk solar imaging. We specifically validated the dynamic performance of the MOF within its magnetic assembly, designed for satellite mounting on a Falcon 9 launch. Additionally, we characterize the spectral transmission of our potassium-based MOF as a function of heating temperature.

Items.Authors: Chris Albert, Jonathon Hunacek, Hien Nguyen, Ritoban Basu Thakur, Charles Bradford, Peter Day, Pierre Echternach, Byeong Ho Eom, Logan Foote, Marc Foote, Elijah Kane, Steve Hailey-Dunsheath, Reinier Janssen, Henry LeDuc
Items.Title: Spatial mapping and capacitor trimming developments to improve usable pixel yield in PRIMA FIRESS kilo-pixel arrays
Items.Abstract: The Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA) will use 8 kilo-pixel kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays in its spectrometer module (FIRESS). We present an improved resonant frequency to spatial position mapping system designed to preserve each device’s mapping after transferring it from the mapping apparatus to the flight housing. With these capabilities, we are also able to improve the usable pixel yield on an array by separating resonances that collide in frequency space. This is done by identifying overlapping resonators and laser trimming the capacitive element on one of the conflicting KIDs to shift its resonant frequency.

Items.Authors: David J. Erskine, Jerry Edelstein, Andrew W. Howard, Samuel P. Halverson, Martin M. Sirk, Edward H. Wishnow
Items.Title: Spectrograph point spread function characterization using a sine comb generator: testing on the Keck Planet Finder spectrograph
Items.Abstract: We describe a technique for spectrograph characterization. An inexpensive Michelson interferometer, fiber connected, creates sine combs that illuminate every pixel of every spectrograph order across its bandwidth. How the sine comb magnitude varies spatially across a detector chip measures how the Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) of a spectrograph varies, which informs the point spread function (PSF) width or spectral resolution. This method senses the PSF in regions in between lines of spectral lamps, or between laser frequency comb spikes. This works for spectrographs of any resolution, including those that cannot resolve laser frequency combs (LFC). We used a Michelson with multiple (sequential) interferometer delays, creating selectable comb pitches proportional to the delay, to map out the Keck Planet Finder (KPF) spectrograph PSF resolution versus (X) wavelength and (Y) order on the detector chip during engineering tests at UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory in early 2022.

Items.Authors: Kenneth McCracken, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Mark Mueller, Daniel Baldwin, Colby Jurgenson, William Podgorski
Items.Title: Spectrograph vacuum chamber GMT-consortium large earth finder (G-CLEF)
Items.Abstract: The GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF) is a fiber-fed, optical echelle spectrograph that will be a first light instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). G-CLEF is a general-purpose echelle spectrograph with precision radial velocity (PRV) capability. The mechanical design of the spectrograph vacuum chamber is an important component that contributes to G-CLEF’s required stability. This paper discusses the various mechanical, thermal, and vacuum performance contributors to the vacuum chamber design. Additionally, the final acceptance tests, internal lab preparations for receiving the chamber and continued chamber testing after arrival are discussed.

Items.Authors: Fabio Rossi, Guido Agapito, Alfio Puglisi, Bernadett Stadler, Daniele Vassallo, Cédric Taïssir Héritier , Enrico Pinna, Jean Pierre Veran, Giulia Carlà, Lorenzo Busoni, Alessio Turchi, Lorenzo Monti, Cédric Plantet, Luca Cortese, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Francesco Maio, Davide Fedele, Kathryn Jackson, Maaike van Kooten, Lorenzo Merli, Marco Bonaglia, Greta Benigni, Edoardo Bellone de Grecis, Pietro Ferraiuolo, Matteo Menessini
Items.Title: SPECULA: adoption, developments, and use cases of a scalable adaptive optics simulation framework
Items.Abstract: SPECULA is a robust, object-oriented framework for end-to-end Adaptive Optics (AO) simulation in Python. Designed for efficiency and scalability, it features native GPU support (CuPy) for high performance on single-node and HPC environments, and facilitates hybrid simulation via seamless Laboratory interfaces.  This contribution reports on SPECULA's growing adoption, its functional extensions, and diverse use cases. The framework is now adopted in major projects, including MATTO, REVOLT and the ESO ELT instruments MORFEO, ANDES, and HARMONI. Ongoing developments feature the addition of Fresnel Propagation, refined HPC and Lab interfaces, and the introduction of a Design GUI. Specialized research applications include PSF Reconstruction with Neural Networks, Cascading Simulations, laboratory efforts for the Petalometer/Cascading bench, and modeling for Optical communication.  These advancements confirm SPECULA as a scalable and versatile platform for current and future AO research.

Items.Authors: Elijah K. Anakalea-Buckley, Daniel Echeverri, Herrick Chang, Joel F. Shields, Nemanja Jovanovic, Ashley Baker, Michael Langmayr, Dimitri Mawet
Items.Title: Status update on the tip/tilt pointing control system of the Keck HISPEC instrument
Items.Abstract: The High-Resolution Infrared Spectrometer for Exoplanet Characterization (HISPEC) is a high-resolution near-infrared spectrograph scheduled for installation at Keck in 2027. HISPEC includes a fiber-nulling mode that requires extremely low tip/tilt jitter (<2 mas RMS). The Keck adaptive optics system delivers ~6 mas RMS, HISPEC incorporates a second-stage tip/tilt loop to meet these stability demands. This subsystem uses a fast-steering mirror driven by a custom multi-kHz SPI control board, a high-speed acquisition and tracking camera operating to 1 kHz, and accelerometers on the telescope to sense and mitigate vibration via feedforward control. Timing-jitter tests show stable performance (<2%) for both the FSM and ATC. This paper outlines the system architecture, presents initial laboratory results, and reports early vibration measurements from the accelerometer system, highlighting relevance for ground-based adaptive optics facilities.

Items.Authors: Changhua Liu, Junlin Ma, Zhiyi Wang
Items.Title: Structural design and analysis of large tracking mounting for astronomical observation
Items.Abstract: Due to the astronomical tracking mount is equipped with the telescope with a large aperture, heavy weight and asymmetric center of gravity, and with the center of gravity changes comes different pitch and azimuth, so the traditional rotating platform structure of the tracking mounting is difficult to achieve high pointing accuracy. Through modeling and analysis, the tracking mount is achieved by combining rotary table bearings and deep groove ball bearings, effectively avoiding the influence of the change of the load center of gravity on the pointing accuracy. Eventually, the turntable speed can reach more than 2 degrees per second, the positioning error is ≤10 arcseconds, and the positioning accuracy is ≤1 arcsecond. It is now deployed at the Lhasa Observatory for astronomical observation.

Items.Authors: Yoshimi Rokugawa, Kenta Sakabe, Yoshihiko Saito, Hideki Takami
Items.Title: Study of an atmospheric turbulence prediction method using a wavefront sensor for uplink laser satellite communication at KgOGS-1 in NICT
Items.Abstract: Laser satellite communication is emerging as a method for high-speed, high-capacity data transfer. The National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) is working to achieve bidirectional laser satellite communication links exceeding 10 Gbps between geostationary satellites and optical ground stations (OGS) using the Engineering Test Satellite-9 (ETS-9). However, atmospheric turbulence—which degrades signal quality—remains a significant challenge. Adaptive optics is a key solution: while downlink distortions can be corrected at the ground station, uplinks require complex pre-compensation and turbulence prediction, especially considering point-ahead angles. At NICT, an adaptive optics system installed at the Koganei 1 m OGS (KgOGS-1m) is being used for research and development in laser communication. This presentation outlines NICT’s approach to predicting uplink turbulence profiles using downlink wavefront and wind data, and verifies its effectiveness.

Items.Authors: Yosuke Minowa, Noelia Martinez Rey, Yuhei Takagi, Yoshito Ono, Yoko Tanaka, Takamasa Bando, Masayuki Akiyama
Items.Title: Subaru Laser Guide Star Facility upgrade for the LTAO mode: 4 LGS with a diffractive optical element
Items.Abstract: The Subaru laser guide star (LGS) system has been upgraded by implementing the high-power laser and a new laser relay system. The increased laser return photon can also bring a new capability of generating multiple LGSs by splitting the laser beam, which will realize a new Laser Tomography Adaptive Optics mode.   We have recently installed a series of Diffractive Optical Elements (DOE) in the laser beam relay light path just before entering the laser launching telescope. The DOE can split the single laser beam into four to generate an asterism of the 4 LGSs. There are 4 DOEs installed in a filter wheel to generate the asterism with the diameter of 10, 20, 30, and 40 arcsec.   In this presentation, we will provide an overview of the LLT upgrade with the DOEs, introduce the alignment and calibration strategy in the laboratory, and present the on-sky characterizations of the 4 LGSs.

Items.Authors: Hans-Peter Doerr, Mathias Ball, Falk Hoffmann, Michael Kehr, Tom Löwinger, Lars Maiwald, Ralf J. Neubert, Hemanth Pruthvi, Veronika Schaffenroth, Michael Sigwarth, Michael Unseld, Johannes U. Winkler, Markus Roth
Items.Title: TauFOS: Faint Object Spectrograph for the 2-Meter Alfred Jensch Telescope in Tautenburg, Germany
Items.Abstract: The Tautenburg Faint Object Spectrograph (TauFOS) is a low-resolution (R=2000) spectrograph optimized for the blue  wavelength range (370-540nm), which has been commissioned in April 2026 at the 2-Meter Alfred Jensch Telescope of the Thüringer Landessternwarte (TLS), Tautenburg, Germany. TauFOS is based on a custom, very efficient transmission grating used in first order, a set of custom lens objectives for collimator and camera and a blue-optimized 2k × 2k CCD detector. The instrument is fiber-fed with three channels for object, sky and simultaneous wavelength calibration. A dedicated frontend has been developed which includes a fast tip-tilt image stabilization system to minimize losses by guiding erros and seeing and to stabilize light injection into the fiber. Data from the commissioning campaign shows a performance en par with expectations. TauFOS will initially be used for a program targeting faint binary Stars.

Items.Authors: Oscar Gonzalez, Martin A. Barstow, Stephen P. Todd, Ariadna Z. Calcines Rosario, Paul Eccleston, Fraser Clarke, David Pearson, Stephen Watson
Items.Title: Technologies for a UVMOS/IFU instrument for Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will be the next NASA-led flagship mission, following HST, JWST and Roman. Through support from UKSA, UK community studies of different instrument options defined in the NASA HWO studies are now underway. One of them is a UV Multi-Object Spectrograph instrument. The work is examining the current requirements for such an instrument in line with its science objectives, identifying the key technical capabilities and TRL levels to achieve them. These evaluations are done also considering the potential of an Integral Field Unit Spectrograph instrument for the mission. This work seeks to establish potential international partnerships to fill technology gaps and identify required activities for raising TRLs to flight levels, to bring such a powerful capabilities in HWO to a reality. This paper reports on this ongoing study and its future plans.

Items.Authors: Haroldo Lorenzo Hernández, Mehdi Bouzit, José Alberto Rubiño-Martín, Angeles Pérez-de-Taoro, Roger Hoyland, María F. Gómez-Reñasco, Marta Aguiar-Gonzalez, David Díaz-Martín, Ricardo T. Génova-Santos, Roberto Puddu, Afrodisio Vega-Moreno, Angela María Arriero-López, Alessandro Fasano, Roke Cepeda-Arroita, Rafael Rebolo, Carlos Hernández-Monteagudo, Debabrata Adak
Items.Title: Tenerife Microwave Spectrometer (TMS): mechanical design, manufacture, and preliminary AIV for the QUIJOTE CMB experiment in Tenerife
Items.Abstract: The Tenerife Microwave Spectrometer (TMS) is a cryogenic radiometer developed for the QUIJOTE facility to measure absolute spectral distortions in the 10–20 GHz band. This work presents the complete mechanical development of the instrument, from design and manufacturing to integration and verification (AIV). The mechanical architecture includes the cold structure, support system, cryostat interfaces, and precision opto-mechanical assemblies, all optimized using detailed FEM analyses. Completed manufacturing and preliminary AIV tests, including alignment metrology and multiple cryogenic cooldown campaigns, are used to assess compliance with the structural and thermal requirements. These results evaluate the readiness of the TMS mechanical system for deployment as a fully qualified cryogenic instrument at the Teide Observatory.

Items.Authors: Dong Liu
Items.Title: Terahertz high-sensitivity SIS mixer based on Nb–AlN–NbN hybrid superconducting tunnel junctions
Items.Abstract: The terahertz band is crucial for observing the cold, dark universe and plays a pivotal role in cutting-edge scientific research. High-sensitivity superconductor–insulator–superconductor (SIS) mixers are essential detectors for terahertz astronomical telescopes and interferometric arrays. Compared to the commonly used classical Nb/AlOx/Nb superconducting tunnel junction, the Nb/AlN/NbN hybrid superconducting tunnel junction has a higher energy gap voltage and can achieve a higher critical current density. This makes it particularly promising for the development of ultra-wideband, high-sensitivity coherent detectors or mixers in various scientific research fields. We will present a superconducting SIS mixer based on Nb/AlN/NbN parallel-connected twin junctions, which has a bandwidth extending up to 490 GHz–720 GHz. The best achieved double-sideband noise temperature is below three times the quantum noise level.

Items.Authors: Sanchit Sabhlok, Ewan Douglas, Solvay A. Blomquist, Debstuti Biswas, Maggie Y Kautz, Simran Agarwal, Alexandra Kupersmith, Adam Schilperoort, Stephanie Rinaldi, Kelsey L Miller, Kyle van Gorkum, Corey Fucetola, Patrick Ingraham, Heejoo Choi, Daewook Kim
Items.Title: Testing of machine learning phase retrieval algorithms on the Tiny Observatory for Telescope Optimization (TOTO) testbed
Items.Abstract: Phase retrieval techniques are utilized to correct low order aberrations originating from misalignments of the optical system in space based telescope concepts. Traditional phase retrieval involves observation of the Point Spread Function (PSF) and a diversity measurement, usually focus diversity although other measures are possible, to reconstruct the incident wavefront at the science detector. We consider a Machine Learning Phase Retrieval model trained originally on simulated data, and then augmented with real focus diversity data from the Tiny Observatory for Telescope Optimization (TOTO) testbed at the University of Arizona. We then compare the performance of the Machine Learning Phase Retrieval method with a traditional phase retrieval technique and assess the difference in performance.

Items.Authors: Pierluca Sangiorgi, Mattia Corpora, Andrea Abba, Ismam Abu, Milvia Capalbi, Vito Conforti, Giovanni Contino, Carmelo Gargano, Fulvio Gianotti, Fabio Paolo Lo Gerfo, Davide Mollica, Giovanni Pareschi, Valerio Pastore, Salvatore Scuderi, Giuseppe Sottile, Gino Tosti
Items.Title: The AIV/AIT Control Software Client for the ASTRI Mini-Array Cherenkov Camera
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array international collaboration led by the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF) is developing nine Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes to study Galactic and extra-galactic sources at TeV energies. Currently, seven out of nine telescope structures are deployed at the Teide Observatory in Tenerife, Canary Islands.Two of these telescopes are also equipped with their SiPM based Cherenkov Camera and are now under Commissioning and Science Verification Phase operations. This work presents the AIV/AIT Control Software Client designed and developed ad-hoc in order to manage all the functionalities exported by the Local Control Software of the Cherenkov Camera. It has been integrated into the ASTRI Mini-Array IT infrastructure at Teide to be used both during AIV/AIT activities and routine observing runs.

Items.Authors: Stephen A. Smee, Robert H. Barkhouser, Mirek Golebiowski, John C. Wilson, Randolph P. Hammond, Nancy J. Chanover
Items.Title: The ASPEN optical bench preliminary design
Items.Abstract: We present the preliminary optical bench design for the ARC SPectrograph for Echelle iNvestigations (ASPEN), a new optical echelle slit spectrograph for the Astrophysical Research Consortium (ARC) 3.5 m Telescope at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico. ASPEN is a visible echelle spectrograph covering 340–10000 nm with user-selectable resolving power from 32,000 to 64,000. Its white-pupil optical layout offers high efficiency through bandpass-optimized materials and coatings in separate blue and red channels. A low-expansion carbon-fiber bench and thermal enclosure provide excellent thermal stability, and a vacuum-enclosed echelle grating eliminates instability due to temporal variations in atmospheric pressure. In this paper, we describe the requirements, goals, and design considerations for the optical bench, and present the resulting optical and opto-mechanical designs.

Items.Authors: Joss Guy, Alexandre Jeanneau, Jürgen Schmoll, Ariadna Calcines Rosario, Robert J. Harris, Jennifer King, Mathilde Jauzac, Simon Morris, Florence Laurent, Rémi Giroud, Johan Richard, Davor Krajnović
Items.Title: The blue multi unit spectroscopic explorer (BlueMUSE) on the VLT: spectrograph optomechanical design concept
Items.Abstract: BlueMUSE is a blue-optimised, medium spectral resolution, panoramic integral field spectrograph under development for the Very Large Telescope (VLT). With an optimised transmission down to 350 nm, spectral resolution of R~3500 on average across the wavelength range, and a large FoV (1 arcmin²), BlueMUSE will open up a new range of galactic and extragalactic science cases facilitated by its specific capabilities. Following the successful completion of the Phase A review in Spring 2025, which established the conceptual design, the instrument will soon fully enter its design phase (Phase B). When built, the instrument will employ 16 identical integral field units (IFUs), each containing a dedicated spectrograph. Here we present the optomechanical design of these spectrographs, developed further prior to the commencement of Phase B.

Items.Authors: Daniel J. Patnaude, Ralph Kraft, Gerrit Schellenberger, Thomas Gauron, Paul Nulsen, Grant Tremblay, Bradley Bissell, Ken Gage, Matthew Dahmer
Items.Title: The Chandra X-ray Observatory high resolution camera: a 2026 status report
Items.Abstract: he High Resolution Camera (HRC) is one of the two prime instruments aboard the Chandra X-ray Observatory. It provides users with arcsecond imaging, microsecond timing resolution, and is the only active X-ray instrument with sensitivity to X-rays below the carbon edge. When combined with Chandra's insertable transmission gratings, the HRC offers resolving power > 1000 in the 70 - 200 eV band. Over its 25 year lifetime, the HRC has enabled transformative studies of neutron star kicks, superluminal jets, and the properties of exoplanet host stars. The Chandra HRC is now the benchmark for long duration studies of microchannel plates in a space environment. Here we discuss the current state of the HRC, including the operational status of the two cameras, the recovery efforts associated with two significant anomalies which have occurred in the last 5 years, and changes to HRC operations which have enabled its continued success.

Items.Authors: Mattia Corpora, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Federico Russo, Ismam Abu, Andrea Bulgarelli, Pietro Bruno, Milvia Capalbi, Vito Conforti, Giovanni Contino, Alessandro Costa, Carmelo Gargano, Fulvio Gianotti, Alessandro Grillo, Isaías Huerta, Fabio Paolo Lo Gerfo, Fabrizio Lucarelli, Teresa Mineo, Edgar Molina, Davide Mollica, Kevin Munari, Giovanni Pareschi, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Valerio Pastore, Salvatore Scuderi, Gino Tosti, Giuseppe Sottile
Items.Title: The Cherenkov Camera Supervisor Deployment in the ASTRI Mini-Array SCADA System
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array, led by INAF, is deploying nine dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes for TeV gamma-ray astronomy. Seven structures are already installed at the Teide Observatory, with two equipped with SiPM-based Cherenkov Cameras and active in Commissioning and Science Verification. The Cherenkov Camera Supervisor (CCS) is the software subsystem that controls, monitors, and integrates each Camera within the global SCADA infrastructure. Built on the ACS middleware and the OPC-UA standard, it provides a scalable interface for housekeeping data, configuration, safety interlocks, and operational commands. The CCS has completed extensive validation on multiple testbeds, including real hardware, and current integration with the full SCADA system shows stable interoperability and correct synchronization. This work summarizes the updated CCS architecture and recent deployment results toward full Mini-Array commissioning.

Items.Authors: Karl Kosack, Matthias Füßling, Igor Oya, Mieke Bouwhuis, Maximillian Linhoff, Catherine Boisson, Mathieu Servillat, Bruno Khélifi
Items.Title: The CTAO data model: towards open and FAIR data from a gamma-ray observatory
Items.Abstract: CTAO will be the first very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray observatory to offer open data. Users will receive tables of reconstructed photon-like events, instrument response functions, and automatically produced “quick-look” products like images, spectra, and light curves for known targets and regions of interest. To produce these data products, CTAO will process PBs of raw and simulated data, with periodic re-processing as algorithms improve. To manage the complexity, CTAO is developing data models, formats, and pipelines that ensure FAIR and open access. The data model covers science data from raw to high-level catalogs and internal operations from proposal submission to public release. We will introduce how data are processed, focusing on the data model, its technical implementation, and the efforts to link to wider virtual observatory standards, e.g. those from the IVOA.

Items.Authors: Tomas Krasuski, Gary Muller, Trupti Ranka, Dave Ashby, John Ford, David Zeller, William Schoenell, Jordi Molgo, Barbara Fischer, Marianne Cox
Items.Title: The design and performance of Giant Magellan Telescope Observatory’s primary mirror actuator calibration system employing a hexapod motion stage
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) has developed an Actuator Calibration System (ACS) to calibrate and qualify the Primary Mirror Support Actuators (M1SA) prior to installing them into its M1 active support system. The ACS uses six precision load cells arranged in a hexapod configuration to measure the M1SA’s applied forces and moments. It then calculates the errors, generates correction matrices, and downloads them into each M1SA’s non-volatile memory for correcting the actuator’s applied forces during operations. A unique feature of GMTO’s ACS is its dynamic interface, or Motion Stage, to the M1SA under test. Supported by six electrically driven actuators arranged in a hexapod pattern, this motion stage provides enough travel to exercise each M1SA under test through its range of motion and simulated tracking programs.This paper describes the design and performance of the GMTO M1 ACS.

Items.Authors: Kanchita Klangboonkrong, Caitlyn Altermatt, Lee Bernard, Andrea Bocchieri, Nathaniel Butler, Oliver Carey, John Hartley, Ryan Challener, Kyle Helson, Daniel Kelly, Maura Lally, Edward Leong, Nikole Lewis, Steven Li, Michael Line, Stephen Maher, Lorenzo Mugnai, Peter Nagler, Calvin Barth Netterfield, Vivien Parmentier, Enzo Pascale, Jennifer Patience, Timothy Rehm, Javier Romualdez, Paul Scowen, Gregory Tucker, Ingo Waldmann
Items.Title: The design and performance of the cryogenic receiver for the EXoplanet Climate Infrared TElescope (EXCITE)
Items.Abstract: The EXoplanet Climate Infrared TElescope (EXCITE) is a stratospheric balloon-borne telescope designed to perform phase-resolved spectroscopy of hot Jupiter atmospheres in the 0.8 - 4 um range. EXCITE will fly from a long-duration balloon platform and provide critical insights into atmospheric composition and thermal structure by continuously observing exoplanets through entire orbits.  This presentation details the design and thermal requirements of the EXCITE cryogenic receiver and the cryogenic control electronics. The cryogenic receiver uses two Thales LPT9310 commercial off-the-shelf cryocoolers to cool a spectrograph, an H2RG detector, and accompanying detector readout electronics. We introduce the cryocooler heat rejection system and report the thermal performance from a 2024 engineering flight from Fort Sumner, New Mexico.

Items.Authors: João Canais, António Amorim, Mercedes Filho, Paulo Garcia
Items.Title: The development of a precision metrology system for a movable large structure applied to the WSS/METIS/ELT
Items.Abstract: We here present the development of a precision metrology system, specifically designed for the integration and alignment testing of the WSS subsystem of the first light instrument METIS for the ELT. The procedure involves the use of laser curtains and image processing algorithms to be compared with high-resolution total station measurements, and is applicable to large scale structures requiring high precision metrology.

Items.Authors: Shin'ichi Nagata, Ayumi Asai, Denis P. Cabezas, Tomoya Iju, Gohichi Kimura, Yoshikazu Nakatani, Satoru Ueno, Takaaki Yokoyama
Items.Title: The development of the large-aperture infrared birefringent tunable filter for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope
Items.Abstract: We report the design of a wide-field infrared imaging spectropolarimeter for Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST). The tunable filter consists of a four-stage Lyot filter and a two-stage Michelson filter. The 50 mm clear aperture calcite blocks are sufficient to observe the 120 arc-sec field of view at DKIST. Using these blocks, a bandwidth of 0.08 nm for the FeXIII 1075 nm line can be achieved with a Lyot filter, and a bandwidth of 0.02 nm for the HeI 1083 nm line can be achieved by adding a Michelson to the Lyot filter. A polarizing beam splitter placed at the exit of the Lyot filter enables simultaneous dual-wavelength observation. The design of the Near Infrared Tunable Filter (NIRTF), which uses two sets of this type of birefringent filter, will be explained in detail.

Items.Authors: Aiden S. Zelakiewicz, Dmitry Savransky, Lisa Kaltenegger
Items.Title: The effect of phase angle on biosignature detection with the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: Characterizing the atmospheres of Earth-like planets is a key goal of NASA’s next flagship-class astrophysics mission concept, the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). We simulate HWO observations of an Earth-like exoplanet at varying orbital configurations and perform spectral retrievals to constrain the surface and atmospheric composition. The phase angle, like cloud coverage and surface features, acts as a normalizing factor for the spectra. We explore how including the phase angle as a free parameter affects atmospheric and surface retrievals. We discuss how phase angle, surface spectra, and water clouds can harbor significant degeneracies. This will hinder placing potential biosignature detections into the full context of the planet. Further development of retrieval algorithms is necessary before robust statistical constraints can be achieved for terrestrial planets.

Items.Authors: Daniel Lancaster, Owain Snaith, Stefan Kraus, Jyotirmay Paul, Sorabh Chhabra
Items.Title: The electrical and firmware implementation of BIFROST
Items.Abstract: BIFROST is a four beam combiner and spectrograph in the near-infrared (1-1.7um). This will be a part of the the ASGARD visitor instrument array at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) in Paranal, Chile. To achieve the scientific goals of BIFROST there are over fifty electronic actuators in BIFROST all with their own unique and different power and control requirements. In this paper we will discuss the electrical system of BIFROST. This will include the power management structure, system connections, and the custom firmware and design of some electronic actuators. Primarily the implementation of new fiber switcher module. We will show the initial designs and testing of the electrical system as well as optical justifications for the resolution of the encoder of the fiber switcher. This will then be followed by the implementation on the mountain and possible future upgrades.

Items.Authors: Gert Raskin, Jakob Pember, Christian Schwab, Wim Pessemier, Jesus Pérez Padilla, Muhammad Salman, Julien Storm, Johan Morren, Bart Vandenbussche
Items.Title: The environmental control system of the MARVEL spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The new MARVEL facility consists of four robotic 0.8m telescopes feeding a large Echelle spectrograph for precision radial velocity observations. To achieve our stability goal of 1m/s RV error, the spectrograph opto-mechanics are installed in a large vacuum chamber which is precisely controlled in temperature. The instrument is housed in a nested temperature-controlled room, inside a new dedicated facility building. Here we outline the layout of our vacuum system, and describe the advanced temperature control approach of the spectrograph, vacuum chamber and instrument room.

Items.Authors: Paul P. Plucinsky, Herman L. Marshall, Akos Bogdan, Peter Ratzlaff
Items.Title: The evolution of the ACIS contamination layer on the Chandra X-ray Observatory from 2010 to 2026
Items.Abstract: The Chandra X-ray Observatory (CXO) was launched over 25 years ago and has been delivering spectacular science over the course of its mission. The Advanced CCD Imager Spectrometer (ACIS) is the prime instrument on the satellite, conducting over 90% of the observations. The CCDs operate at a temperature of -120 C and the optical blocking filter (OBF) in front of the CCDs is at a temperature of approximately -60 C. The surface of the OBF has accumulated a layer of contamination over the course of the mission, as it is the coldest surface exposed to the interior of the spacecraft. We have been characterizing the thickness, chemical composition, and spatial distribution of the contamination layer as a function of time over the mission. In this paper, we describe the latest update to the contamination model which consists of a change to the time dependence of the thickness of the O and F layers.

Items.Authors: Nicholas E. Kruczek, Kevin France, Juliana Barstow, Nicholas Nell, Emily Farr, Patrick R. Behr, Paloma López Reyes, Juan Larruquert, Carlos Honrado-Benítez, Alejandro García-Cañas, John Hennessy, Stefan Ulrich
Items.Title: The FLUID sounding rocket: technology test bed for advanced optical coatings and detectors for HWO
Items.Abstract: The Far- and Lyman-Ultraviolet Imaging Demonstrator (FLUID) is a rocket-borne multi-band arcsecond-level ultraviolet (UV) imaging instrument covering four wavelength bands between 92 - 193 nm. Each of FLUID’s channels are comprised of individual telescopes employing wavelength-selecting optical filters; the four channels are co-aligned to create simultaneous FUV images of an astronomical target. FLUID will observe nearby galaxies to characterize the most massive stars, the primary drivers of the chemical and dynamical evolution of galaxies. FLUID accomplishes this science goal while raising the technology readiness level (TRL) of band-selecting UV coatings and solar-blind, UV detector technology needed for next-generation UV facilities such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory. We discuss the development of these novel technologies, including updates on coating performance after environmental aging studies and detector efficiencies, and provide context for how they will support HWO.

Items.Authors: Laird M. Close, Jared Males, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Oli Durney, Maggie Kautz, Adam Fletcher, Victor Gasho, Jamison Noenickx, Douglas Kelly, John Ford, Tommy Salanski, Ian Harley-Trochimczyk, Olivier Guyon, Tiago Giorgetti, Rodrigo Pereira, Claudia Mendes de Oliveira
Items.Title: The GMagAO-X facility ExAO coronagraphic instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope: the first FDR level optomechanical design for an ELT ExAO system
Items.Abstract: Here we outline the current highly advanced design of the facility ExAO instrument GMagAO-X for the 25.4m Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). As we approach our Final Design Review (FDR) we have had to address many interesting challenges to characterize exoplanets in reflected light (capable of IWAs 80% at 0.8um). This drives us to lower the fitting error and requires a 21,000 element DM to allow a 14 cm sampling on the 7x 8.4m (25.4 m diameter) GMT. We have developed a novel “parallel DM” design that was proto-typed and tested on the HCAT testbed at the University of Arizona to allow a seven arm white light fringe (zero OPD) to correct the piston phase errors from the seven GMT segments. We will present for the first time an improved sensitivity 2 stage HDFS piston sensor. FDR is spring 2027.

Items.Authors: Robert Content, Francisco Prada, Enrique Perez, Luca di Fabrizio, Adriano Ghedina, Arturo Manchado, Joonas Viuho, Rosario Cosentino, Guillermo Glez-de-Rivera
Items.Title: The La Palma Quantum Interferometer (LPQI): New optical design method for the Pathfinder cameras and SPAD spectrographs
Items.Abstract: A critical Intensity Interferometry discovery was made: a standard camera optical design does not work, leading to a new designing method. The La Palma Quantum Interferometer collaboration will use the 5 largest telescopes in La Palma to do Intensity Interferometry. Design of 2 cameras for the TNG and NOT telescopes were done in the standard way and with the new method. Our SPAD detectors have a sensitive area covering only 3.5% of each pixel. Two methods were studied to largely increase the transmission, unusual microlens arrays and taking advantage of sensitive areas clustering. In Intensity Interferometry, the S/N is independent of the bandwidth. We intend to place Echelle spectrographs on all 5 telescopes each giving at least 10,000 bands increasing the S/N by >100. A new SPAD detector is under development (goals of 1000x1000 pixels and >90% fill factor). A design was made for the first spectrograph on the ING.

Items.Authors: Guillermo González-de-Rivera, Álvaro Quintana, Sergio López-Buedo, Kashif Buland, Juan Antonio Leñero, Ángel Rodríguez, Carmen Vélez, Robert Content, Luca Difrabizio, Francisco Prada
Items.Title: The La Palma Quantum Interferometer (LPQI): readout electronics for the LPQI-Pathfinder SPAD detector
Items.Abstract: Precise sub-nanosecond timing is critical in SPAD-based instrumentation. The LPQI-Pathfinder readout system adopts a dual-FPGA architecture: a front-end FPGA positioned within centimeters of the 64×64 I2CASS SPAD array and a back-end FPGA integrated into the acquisition computer. This partition minimizes complexity and power (<2 W) inside the detector while enabling hardware-accelerated data handling. The front-end decodes AER output and performs timestamping using Artix UltraScale+ deserializers synchronized via a White Rabbit timing system, achieving 500 ps resolution and sub-nanosecond synchronization across detectors. Data transfer relies on a 6 Gbps Aurora link over copper to the back-end FPGA, which bridges Aurora to PCIe Gen3 and Gigabit Ethernet, with future extensions for real-time processing.

Items.Authors: Eran Ofek, Sagi Ben-Ami, David Polishook, Enrico Segre, Alexander Krassilchtchikov
Items.Title: The Large Array Survey Telescope (LAST)
Items.Abstract: The Large Array Survey Telescopes (LAST) is a cost-effective, wide-field optical array designed for high-cadence exploration of the variable and transient sky, located at the Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory in the Negev Desert, Israel. LAST will consist of 72 units of 28-cm telescopes covering a combined FOV of 533 deg² and 4.4 Gpix system.

Items.Authors: Nina Brown, Chad F. Bender, Andrew Monson, Keita Maekawa, Sonja O. T. Choi, Joel Berkson, Christian Schwab, Lisa Prato, Roger Angel
Items.Title: The Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope: CSHELL revitalization and characterization
Items.Abstract: The Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope (LFAST) utilizes large arrays of small, individual telescopes and fiber-fed optics for high resolution spectroscopy. LFAST will feed two spectrographs; this poster will focus on the Cryogenic Echelle Spectrograph (CSHELL), which observes in the near-IR at 1080-1700 nm. CSHELL was previously operated through the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) from 1992-2016, and has since been decommissioned. However, the still-functioning instrument offers the LFAST project a promising solution for low-cost, high-resolution spectroscopy. This paper will present results for detector and instrument characterization, as well as progress on an automated data reduction pipeline.

Items.Title: The Lazuli Space Observatory’s ExtraSolar Coronagraph
Items.Abstract: The Lazuli Space Observatory, part of the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Observatory System, is a 3-meter class astronomical observatory designed for rapid-response observations and precision astrophysics across visible to near-infrared wavelengths with science capabilities that will be transformative in this decade. Onboard Lazuli is a high-contrast imaging system, the ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC), that is designed to enable direct imaging and characterization of exoplanets and circumstellar debris disks around nearby stars. The ESC hosts an ultra-high-contrast adaptive optics (AO) system and vector vortex coronagraph (VVC) to enable high-contrast imaging with raw contrasts of 1e-8 and post-processed contrasts approaching 1e-9. In this presentation, we will provide a technical overview of the ESC design and development underway at the University of Arizona and insight into the unique role Lazuli’s ExtraSolar Coronagraph plays in the current astrophysical landscape.

Items.Authors: Sriprasanna Srivalli Annadevara, Hanna Kellermann, Lenard Spallek, Florian Lang, Jörg Schlichter, Hans-Joachim Hess, Luis Neumeier, Helmut Kravcar, Ralf Bender
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: Cryostat control software tests and lessons learned
Items.Abstract: The Multi-Adaptive Optics Imaging Camera for Deep Observations (MICADO) is the first light ESO Extremely-Large-Telescope (ELT) Instruments, and is currently in the integration and test phase of the project. The MICADO instrument aims to generate high-resolution images of the Universe at near-infrared wavelengths, which requires maintaining a stable vacuum environment at 82 K inside the MICADO cryostat. To fulfil this requirement and for safety reasons, Beckhoff PLC-based control software was developed and successfully tested. This software communicates with nearly 200 sensors and controllers simultaneously to maintain the cryostat environment. This paper discusses the cryostat control software tests, outcomes, lessons learned, direction of future updates and methodologies used to solve the few open issues systematically. It also discusses the adaption of the Beckhoff HTML5-based HMI toolkit developed by ESO to the MICADO cryostat-control software.

Items.Authors: Fanny Chemla, Mathieu Cohen, Eric Gendron, Karim Hussein, Olivier Dupuis, Julien Gaudemard, Frédéric Chapron, Kevin Cloiseau, Yann Clénet, Richard Davies
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: opto-mechanical assembly, alignment, and testing of the SCAO module
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the ELT first-light imager, is designed to operate at the diffraction limit of the telescope, thanks to two adaptive optics (AO) modes: SCAO and MCAO. The SCAO module has entered the AIT phase after its final design review. In this paper, we report the opto-mechanical status and performance of the manufactured subsystems. These are tested in a temporary set-up referred to as the “β-flat configuration,” while the subsequent “flat” and “final” configurations are prepared in parallel. We also present a method allowing the alignment of opto-mechanics on carbon benches, despite the low flexibility of such structures due to predefined inserts. Furthermore, we explain how we optimize the optical performance, by measuring each element’s wavefront error with a ZYGO interferometer, and then by adjusting or remachining mechanical parts whenever stress points induced by the mounting are revealed.

Items.Authors: Jörg Schlichter, Luis Neumeier, Joost van den Born, Michael Wegner
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: Software control of tracking devices.
Items.Abstract: MICADO is the designated first-light instrument of ESO's ELT. In its non-AO part it is equipped with two tracking devices, namely an atmospheric dispersion corrector (ADC) and a combined de-rotator/co-rotator system. These devices have to follow the on-sky-movements of the telescope with high accuracy and in complete synchronicity. In contrast to older instruments, this is achieved via a software-only control approach.    We describe here the overall control architecture of the system, the data-flow from the telescope down to the PLC-based motor control, and the design of our control software. In addition, we present a number of measurements to prove the functionality of the chosen software approach.

Items.Authors: Birgitta Müller, Anna Monna, Florian Lang, Frank Grupp, Ralf Bender
Items.Title: The MICADO first-light imager for the ELT: integration and alignment of MICADO's main selection mechanism on a coordinate measuring machine
Items.Abstract: Inside the cryostat of MICADO, the first light instrument for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), the switching between the four operational modes is enabled by the cryogenic Main Selection Mechanism (MSM). Consisting of a main support structure and a rotating platform carrying the MICADO Low Resolution Imager, Spectrometer and Pupil Imager modules, the mechanism components were completely manufactured and procured in 2025. In this paper we present the results of the integration and alignment of the Pupil Imager and Spectrograph as well as the MSM warm setup. Furthermore, we present the results of the completely integrated and aligned mechanism, including all final cryogenic components prior to the delivery to MPE, the MICADO Project lead Institute, for its integration inside the instrument cryostat.

Items.Authors: Shumei Jia
Items.Title: The operation and data processing of the Einstein Probe FXT Science Data Center
Items.Abstract: The Einstein Probe (EP) is equipped with two types of scientific payloads, the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) and the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT). The EP-FXT Science Data Center (SDC) is established in the Institute of High Energy Physics (IHEP) and is responsible for the FXT data processing. The FXT SDC has maintained a continuous operation since the EP’s launch on January 9, 2024. It has provided the standard data products, released the data analysis software and calibration database, and supported the science users in conducting scientific research. In this paper, we present a systematic and comprehensive overview of the primary workflows and key tasks of the FXT science data center.

Items.Authors: Andrea A. Bulgarelli, Vito Conforti, Mauricio Araya, Gabriele Barni, Ciro Bigongiari, Pietro Giuseppe Bruno, Milvia Capalbi, Martina Cardillo, Guillermo Andres Rodriguez Castillo, Osvaldo Catalano, Antonio Compagnino, Mattia Corpora, Alessandro Costa, Silvia Crestan, Giancarlo Cusumano, Antonino D'Aì, Valentina Fioretti, Stefano Gallozzi, Stefano Germani, Gonzalo Gallo, Fulvio Gianotti, Valentina Giordano, Andrea Giuliani, Alessandro Grillo, Isaías Huerta, Federico Incardona, Simone Iovenitti, Nicola La Palombara, Valentina La Parola, Marco Landoni, Saverio Lombardi, Fabrizio Lucarelli, Maria Concetta Maccarone, Rachele Millul, Teresa Mineo, Gabriela Montenegro, Davide Mollica, Kevin Munari, Antonio Pagliaro, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Giovanni Pareschi, Valerio Pastore, Matteo Perri, Fabio Pintore, Pat Romano, Federico Russo, Ricardo Zanmar Sánchez, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Francesco Gabriele Saturni, Nestor Sayes, Eva Sciacca, Sebastiano Spinello, Vitalii Sliusar, Salvo Scuderi, Alessandro Tacchini, Vincenzo Testa, Gino Tosti, Antonio Tutone, Stefano Vercellone, Roland Walter, Luca Zampieri
Items.Title: The SCADA Software System of the ASTRI Mini-Array: Architecture, Control Workflow, and Operational Integration
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array consists of nine dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes operated remotely at Teide Observatory. Its operations rely on a distributed SCADA system that supervises, controls, and monitors all on-site assemblies. A key element is the Startup System, which manages initialization and configuration of services before observations. Built on ALMA Common Software, SCADA provides coordinated control via the Central Control System, handling Scheduling Blocks, alarms, and safe-state transitions. A web-based HMI offers unified access for engineering and night-time operations, while a dedicated Startup System HMI supports deep troubleshooting of observing subsystems. Monitoring data from OPC-UA, ACS components, and custom collectors follow ICD-defined schemas and stream via AVRO to InfluxDB and Cassandra. SCADA interfaces with data acquisition and online quality tools to ensure robust, efficient scientific operations. This work presents SCADA’s architecture and workflows.

Items.Authors: Jamie Soon, Christopher Lidman, Anais Moller, Ian Price
Items.Title: The Siding Spring Observatory Transient Factory and Alert System
Items.Abstract: We present the Siding Spring Observatory Transient Factory (SSOTF) and the Siding Spring Observatory Alert System, these systems are designed to draw together different photometric and spectroscopic telescopes available at Siding Spring Observatory, New South Wales, Australia. The system is designed to rapidly observe targets of interest without human interaction and can utilise automated sequential observations and data reduction processes.    We will present results from the first months of on-sky operations, coinciding with the start of the ANU 2.3m 2026A semester and operations of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time of the Rubin Observatory.

Items.Authors: Donghua Zhao, Lei Wang, Wenxin Wang, Zhenqing Jia, Zhixing Ling, Chen Zhang, Weimin Yuan, Junsheng Cheng, Shuangnan Zhang
Items.Title: The simulations and experiments on the electron diverter of the Wide-field X-ray telescope onboard Einstein Probe mission
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) is the X-ray focusing telescope employing the lobster-eye type micro-pore optics onboard the Einstein Probe (EP) mission of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. By performing simulations, we find that low-energy electrons (1-1000 keV) can cause high background count rate on the detector of WXT. Therefore, each WXT module is equipped with an electron diverter as previous X-ray telescopes. We will present our simulations and experiments on the deflection efficiency of the diverter for electrons.

Items.Authors: Maud P. Langlois, Valentin Fonteneau, camille Graf, Gil Moretto, Rafael rebolo, Jeff Kuhn
Items.Title: The Small ExoLife Finder Telescope (SELF): extreme OA performance for a sparse aperture nulling telescope dedicated to exoplanets imaging in reflected light
Items.Abstract: Detecting an telluric exoplanets is extremely challenging with current technology because it requires a sensitive tele-scope and instrument that can measure the planet's reflected optical and infrared light, while distinguishing this from the star's scattered light and the terrestrial thermal noise background. This requires highly accurate adaptive optics, a coronagraphic system, and a specially designed sparse aperture dedicated nulling telescope. We present here new strate-gies for building such a telescope with large circular segments using adaptive optics correction independently for each of these segments coupled with cophasing the segments. In this context we propose to derive the segments phase error using the the Mach-Zehnder wavefront sensing technology we have patented. These measurements need to be coupled with high precision wavefront sensing for Extreme-AO. We describe our end-to-end simulations of the XAO and high contrast performences.

Items.Authors: Yukari M. Toyoda, Takayuki Kotani, Aoi Takahashi, Riku Urago, Takeru Nakajima, Ko Hosokawa, Masayuki Kuzuhara, Takuya Takarada, Motohide Tamura, Jun Nishikawa, Akitoshi Ueda, Teruyuki Hirano, Takahiro Nagayama, Takuma Kokusho, Eiko Kozaki, Takahiro Sumi, Daisuke Suzuki, Hibiki Yama, Tomoyasu Yamamuro, Naoshi Murakami, Urumi Hayashi, Moe Suzuki
Items.Title: The South Africa Near-Infrared Doppler (SAND) instrument: current status of system integration and performance verification
Items.Abstract: The South Africa Near-Infrared Doppler (SAND) instrument is a high-dispersion, fiber-fed spectrograph designed for precise radial velocity measurements in the near-infrared. Covering the z–Y bands (849–1090 nm) at a resolution of ~65,000, it will be installed at SAAO and mainly operated on the 1.8-m PRIME telescope, with additional use on IRSF. SAND aims to detect habitable-zone planets around nearby M-dwarfs (<3500 K, <7 pc) with RV precision below 2 m/s and to survey gas-giant planets around young stars within 100 pc with precision better than 10 m/s. Its cryogenic system and stabilized Fabry–Pérot etalon ensure high RV accuracy. Access to numerous young stellar associations in the southern sky further enhances its scientific capability. Most components have been fabricated, and the project is now in the integration and performance verification phase.

Items.Authors: Kyle J. Van Gorkom, Ramya M. Anche, Kian Milani, Saraswathi Kalyani Subramanian, Adam Schilperoort, Kevin Derby, Emory Jenkins, Jaren Ashcraft, Patrick Ingraham, Daewook Kim, Heejoo Choi, Olivier Durney, Ewan S. Douglas
Items.Title: The Space Coronagraph Optical Bench (SCoOB): 11. status of ongoing upgrades and vacuum performance
Items.Abstract: The space coronagraph optical bench (SCoOB) previously demonstrated ~10^-9 narrowband and ~10^-8 broadband contrast performance. In the last year, the testbed has undergone major upgrades, including a 100%-yield BMC Kilo-C deformable mirror, a black silicon pupil stop, wedged quarter wave plate retarders and polarizers, improved sensor cooling, and a microfabricated field stop. In this work, we present the contrast performance of the testbed after these upgrades for three different coronagraph architectures: a) a vector vortex mask with polarization filtering, b) a triple grating vector vortex mask with and without polarization filtering, and c) a carbon nanotube shaped pupil mask. We report the latest broadband performance of the testbed using multi-band electric field conjugation for improved broadband control and wavefront stabilization via Lyot low-order wavefront sensing and control, as well as our progress in pushing toward bluer wavelengths.

Items.Authors: Kevin Zhang Derby, Kian Milani, Kyle J. Van Gorkom, Ramya M. Anche, Saraswathi Subramanian, Adam A. Schilperoort, Jaren N. Ashcraft, Irina I. Stefan, Heejoo Choi, Lori B. Harrison, Daewook Kim, Ewan S. Douglas
Items.Title: The Space Coronagraph Optical Bench (SCoOB): 9. improvements to adjoint electric field conjugation and a demonstration in broadband light
Items.Abstract: We report on recent development in using adjoint electric field conjugation (aEFC) on the University of Arizona’s Space Coronagraph Optical Bench (SCoOB). In its current configuration, SCoOB is a charge-6 vector vortex coronagraph outfitted with a Kilo-C microelectromechanical systems deformable mirror capable of achieving sub-10^-8 dark hole contrast at visible wavelengths. In this work, we discuss ongoing efforts in improving adjoint model calibration. Using this improved model, we give an updated comparison between aEFC and iEFC for dark hole digging on SCoOB. Finally, we provide the first demonstration of aEFC on SCoOB in broadband light.

Items.Authors: Xiaotian Shen, Xiaojin Sun, Xiaohao ma, Zhengda Li, Jiafeng Zhang, Shengli Sun
Items.Title: The Theoretical Minimum of Gravity Sag for Large-Aperture Space Mirrors: A Linear Algebra Framework
Items.Abstract: Decreasing the gravity sag of large space mirrors is critical to ensuring that ground optical test results are consistent with the mirror’s on-orbit performance. Extensive research has focused on reducing gravity sags by improving support structures. We show that gravity sag has a theoretical lower limit that depends only on the stiffness of the mirror itself. In this paper, the mirror surface deformation is expressed as a linear combination of 18 shapes influenced by mount forces, and the minimum RMS gravity sag is therefore obtained analytically via constrained quadratic programming. Only abstract force constraints (equilibrium and symmetry) are required, with no need to model the detailed support structure. The shape of this minimum varies with gravity direction while its RMS value remains constant. Applied to a 2.4 m SiC mirror, the theoretical minimum is 3.72 nm RMS. This minimum can be used for evaluating mirror stiffness and the performance of support designs.

Items.Authors: Will Saunders, Kjetil Dohlen, Dimitri Buffat, Roelof de Jong, Olaf Iwert, David Lee, Andrea Bianco, Ross Zhelem, Etienne Burtin
Items.Title: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope: optical designs for the low-resolution multi-object spectrographs
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope will observe ~30,000 simultaneous low resolution targets, with a resolution R>3000 over 370nm-980nm. This is ~20 times the scale of DESI or PFS, in terms of the total fiber etendue times spectral resolution elements. The ideal camera speeds are of order f/1 or even faster, but the only existing multi-object fiber-fed spectoscopic systems of sufficient speed (MOONS, PFS) have very large catadioptric cameras and dewars, not an attractive solution for the large numbers (40-60) of spectrographs required for WST. Three design solutions are presented; all combine very fast speeds, excellent efficiency and good image quality with relatively simple optics, and straightforward alignment and slit and detector access.

Items.Authors: Mathieu Motte, Vincent Chambouleyron, Romain Fétick, Thierry Fusco, Benoît Neichel, Cedric Taïssir Heritier, Jean-François Sauvage, Nicolas Blind, Christophe Lovis
Items.Title: Theory, simulation, and correction of the atmospheric chromatic refraction effect on XAO instrument
Items.Abstract: The RISTRETTO instrument aims for the observation and characterisation of the atmosphere of the exoplanet Proxima b. This requires an extreme adaptive optics system. At such a level of performance, finer effects emerge. One such phenomenon is the chromatic pupil shift (CPS). This is directly due to the chromatic refraction effect in the atmosphere. Usually, in astronomy, the wavefront sensing is performed at wavelengths different from those of the science path. Due to refraction, the light at the WFS wavelength does not follow the same atmospheric path as that at the science wavelength and therefore experiences slightly different turbulence, inducing an imperfect estimation and a small residual error in the correction.  We propose a direct theoretical model to quantify the impact of CPS on the XAO error budget for instruments such as RISTRETTO, confirm this model through simulations, and provide methods to measure and correct this effect
